specStatements.text: (HT only) Different substances may absorb, transmit, refract or reflect electromagnetic waves in ways that vary with wavelength.
(HT only) Some effects, for example refraction, are due to the difference in velocity of the waves in different substances.
Students should be able to construct ray diagrams to illustrate the refraction of a wave at the boundary between two different media.
(HT only) Students should be able to use wave front diagrams to explain refraction in terms of the change of speed that happens when a wave travels from one medium to a different medium.
Required practical activity 10: investigate how the amount of infrared radiation absorbed or radiated by a surface depends on the nature of that surface.
AT skills covered by this practical activity: AT 1 and 4.
This practical activity also provides opportunities to develop WS and MS. Details of all skills are given in Key opportunities for skills development.

scopeNotes.statement: AT skills covered by this practical activity: AT 1 and 4.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: AT 1 and AT 4 are apparatus-and-technique codes that label the practical work; they are not themselves examinable subject knowledge, so no question asks a student to recall a code number or to say which AT skills a practical covers. The boundary is respected by expressing the skills through the practical items instead: AT 1 (use of appropriate apparatus to make and record measurements) is exercised in q10 and q11, where the detector must be placed at a fixed distance and its reading taken from each surface in turn, and AT 4 (use of apparatus to measure temperature and energy transfer, including safe use of a heat source) is exercised in q11 and q12, where hot water and a radiant heater are used and the warming of the contents is what is measured.

scopeNotes.statement: This practical activity also provides opportunities to develop WS and MS. Details of all skills are given in Key opportunities for skills development.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: This is a signpost to the Working Scientifically and Mathematical Skills lists given elsewhere in the specification, not a piece of physics content, so it carries no questions of its own and no item asks a student to name a WS or MS reference. The boundary is respected by building those opportunities into the Required practical activity 10 items: q11 is a WS item on identifying and controlling variables and on evaluating a method, and q10 and q12 require readings from different surfaces to be compared and ordered, which is the mathematical opportunity this practical offers.

concepts.definition: When a wave meets a substance and its energy is transferred into that substance instead of continuing through it. The wave does not emerge on the far side and the internal energy of the substance increases.

When a wave passes through a substance and emerges on the other side. A substance that transmits a wave lets it carry on, although the velocity of the wave inside the substance may differ from its velocity outside.

When a wave meets a boundary and travels back into the substance it came from rather than entering the new substance. Reflection is a third possibility alongside absorption and transmission, and in general all three happen at once in different proportions.

Whether a particular substance absorbs, transmits, refracts or reflects an electromagnetic wave is not a single fixed property of that substance: it varies with the wavelength of the wave. Glass transmits visible light but absorbs much of the ultraviolet, and brick transmits radio waves but not visible light.

The change of direction of a wave as it crosses the boundary between two substances at an angle to the normal. It is one of the effects a substance can have on a wave, alongside absorbing, transmitting and reflecting it.

concepts.term: Difference in velocity as the cause of refraction
concepts.definition: Some effects, for example refraction, are due to the difference in velocity of the waves in different substances. If a wave had the same velocity in both substances it would cross the boundary without changing direction, however steep the angle.

concepts.term: What changes and what does not at a boundary
concepts.definition: The frequency of a wave is set by its source and does not change when the wave enters a new substance. The velocity does change, so the wavelength must change with it: a wave that slows down has a shorter wavelength in the new substance.

A construction line drawn at right angles to the boundary at the exact point where the ray meets it, usually shown dashed. Every angle in a refraction ray diagram is measured from the normal, never from the boundary itself.

concepts.term: Angle of incidence and angle of refraction
concepts.definition: The angle of incidence is the angle between the incident ray and the normal. The angle of refraction is the angle between the refracted ray and the normal, measured on the far side of the boundary.

concepts.term: Constructing a ray diagram for refraction
concepts.definition: Draw the boundary, add the dashed normal where the ray strikes it, draw the incident ray with an arrow towards the boundary, then draw the refracted ray continuing from that same point with an arrow away from it. A ray entering a substance in which it travels more slowly bends towards the normal; one entering a substance in which it travels faster bends away from the normal; a ray along the normal is not deviated.

A line joining points of a wave that are all in phase with one another, for example all the crests. Wave fronts are drawn at right angles to the direction in which the wave travels, and the spacing between them is the wavelength.

concepts.term: Explaining refraction with a wave front diagram
concepts.definition: When wave fronts meet a boundary at an angle, one end of each front crosses into the new medium before the other end does. If the wave travels more slowly in the new medium that end is held back while the rest of the front is still moving at the old speed, so the front pivots and the whole wave changes direction. The fronts also become closer together, because the wavelength falls with the speed.

Electromagnetic radiation emitted by all objects because of their temperature, and the radiation investigated in Required practical activity 10. A hotter object emits infrared at a greater rate than a cooler one.

concepts.term: How the nature of a surface affects infrared
concepts.definition: A matt black surface is the best absorber of infrared radiation and also the best emitter of it. A shiny, silvered or pale surface is a poor absorber and a poor emitter, and reflects most of the infrared that reaches it. A good absorber is always a good emitter.

A hollow metal cube whose four vertical faces are given different surfaces, for example matt black, matt white, shiny silver and dull grey. Filling it with hot water puts every face at the same temperature, so any difference in the infrared detected must be caused by the nature of the surface.

concepts.term: Control variables in Required practical activity 10
concepts.definition: The nature of the surface is the independent variable, so everything else must be kept the same: the temperature of the water, the distance from the surface to the detector, the orientation of the detector and the time allowed before each reading is taken. Changing any of these alongside the surface makes the comparison invalid.

misconceptions.question: A sheet of glass is transparent. Does that mean it transmits every electromagnetic wave?
misconceptions.correct: No. Glass transmits visible light, but it absorbs a large fraction of the ultraviolet that reaches it, and it is opaque to parts of the infrared range as well.
misconceptions.misconception: If a material looks clear it must let all electromagnetic waves through, because transparency is a property of the material as a whole.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet 'transparent' as an everyday word describing what the eye can see through, so they generalise a statement about one narrow band of wavelengths into a statement about the whole spectrum. Nothing they can see contradicts it.
misconceptions.correction: Transparency is always transparency to a particular range of wavelengths. Different substances may absorb, transmit, refract or reflect electromagnetic waves in ways that vary with wavelength, so glass can be clear to visible light and still absorb ultraviolet.

misconceptions.question: Is ultraviolet radiation always absorbed, whatever substance it meets?
misconceptions.correct: No. What happens to a wave depends on the substance as well as on the wave. Ultraviolet is absorbed strongly by ordinary glass and by skin, but it is transmitted by quartz and by air.
misconceptions.misconception: Each part of the electromagnetic spectrum has one fixed behaviour that it shows everywhere, so ultraviolet is 'the absorbed one' and radio is 'the one that goes through things'.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The spectrum is usually taught as a table of waves with a list of uses attached to each, which invites students to treat behaviour as a property of the wave alone rather than of the wave and substance together.
misconceptions.correction: Absorption, transmission, reflection and refraction are all interactions between a wave and a substance. The same wavelength behaves differently in different substances, and the same substance behaves differently towards different wavelengths.

misconceptions.question: Why does a wave change direction when it crosses a boundary at an angle?
misconceptions.correct: Because the wave has a different velocity in the second substance. Refraction is due to that difference in velocity.
misconceptions.misconception: The wave bounces off the edge of the new substance, or the new substance pushes it sideways as it enters; speed does not come into it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Refraction is met as a bending of light long before the wave picture is available, so students remember the shape of the ray diagram and invent a mechanical cause for it. A ray diagram on its own shows no change of speed anywhere.
misconceptions.correction: The cause is the change of velocity. A wave that travelled at the same velocity in both substances would carry straight on across the boundary, however steeply it met it, and there would be no refraction at all.

misconceptions.question: Light slows down when it enters glass. Does its frequency fall as well?
misconceptions.correct: No. The frequency is set by the source and is unchanged. Because the velocity falls and the frequency stays the same, the wavelength becomes shorter inside the glass.
misconceptions.misconception: Slowing the wave down must slow everything about it, so fewer waves arrive each second and the frequency drops; or else the wavelength is the quantity thought to be fixed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students apply the wave equation without deciding which quantity is fixed by the source and which is fixed by the medium, so whichever of frequency or wavelength they thought of first is held constant.
misconceptions.correction: Waves cannot pile up or vanish at a boundary, so the same number arrives each second on both sides and the frequency is unchanged. With the velocity smaller and the frequency fixed, the wavelength must fall.

misconceptions.question: In a refraction ray diagram, which line is the angle of incidence measured from?
misconceptions.correct: From the normal — the dashed line drawn at right angles to the boundary at the point where the ray strikes it.
misconceptions.misconception: The angle is measured between the ray and the surface of the block, because that is the line already visible on the diagram.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The boundary is a real drawn line and the normal is an added construction line, so students measure from what is already there. The two angles add to 90°, so the error is systematic rather than random.
misconceptions.correction: Every angle in refraction and reflection work is measured from the normal. Always draw the dashed normal first, at the exact point where the ray meets the boundary, and measure both angles from it.

misconceptions.question: A ray enters a glass block along the normal. Does it bend?
misconceptions.correct: No. At an angle of incidence of 0° the ray carries straight on into the glass without changing direction, although it does slow down.
misconceptions.misconception: Light always bends when it goes into glass, because glass is the thing that bends light, so it must bend at 0° too.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every worked example students see uses a slanted ray, so 'entering glass' and 'bending' become welded together. The 0° case is then treated as an exception to be remembered rather than as a consequence of the geometry.
misconceptions.correction: Refraction only turns a wave when one part of the wave front reaches the new substance before the rest. Along the normal the whole front arrives at once, so the wave slows as a whole and travels straight on.

misconceptions.question: Which way round are wave fronts drawn relative to the direction of travel?
misconceptions.correct: At right angles to it. A wave front joins points that are in phase, and the wave advances at right angles to that line.
misconceptions.misconception: Wave fronts run along the direction the wave is travelling, so they can be drawn as arrows or as lines parallel to the ray.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students have spent far longer drawing rays than wave fronts, and a ray points along the direction of travel, so the new kind of line is assumed to point the same way.
misconceptions.correction: Rays and wave fronts are perpendicular to each other. Draw the fronts as a set of parallel lines, like the crests of a water wave, then draw the ray crossing them at 90°.

misconceptions.question: A wave slows down as it enters a new medium. Do the wave fronts get closer together or further apart?
misconceptions.correct: Closer together. The frequency is unchanged and the speed has fallen, so the wavelength — which is the spacing of the fronts — falls too.
misconceptions.misconception: A slower wave has fronts that are further apart, because slowing something down spreads it out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students borrow an image from traffic or from a queue, where things that slow down are imagined to spread out. They also confuse the spacing of the fronts with the time between them, which is unchanged.
misconceptions.correction: The fronts leave the boundary at the same rate as they arrive, because the frequency is fixed. Each front then travels a shorter distance before the next one is produced, so the spacing shrinks in the slower medium.

misconceptions.question: A matt black surface is the best absorber of infrared. Is it a good emitter too?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. A good absorber of infrared radiation is also a good emitter of it, so the matt black face of a Leslie cube gives the largest detector reading.
misconceptions.misconception: Black surfaces soak radiation up and hold on to it, so they are good absorbers but poor emitters; shiny or pale surfaces are thought to give radiation out best.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Absorption is met first, in the context of black clothing feeling hot in the sun, and 'soaking up' suggests keeping. Emission is then treated as a separate, unrelated property of the surface.
misconceptions.correction: Absorption and emission go together: whatever a surface is good at taking in, it is equally good at giving out. Matt black is the best at both and shiny silver is the worst at both.

misconceptions.question: In a Leslie cube experiment, why do the four faces give different readings?
misconceptions.correct: Only because their surfaces are different. The same hot water is behind all four faces, so every face is at the same temperature.
misconceptions.misconception: The surface finish makes no difference to how much radiation an object emits or absorbs; only its temperature and its distance from the detector matter, so objects kept in identical conditions must give identical readings.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students reach for temperature as the cause of anything to do with heating, and the inside of the cube is not visible, so it is easy to imagine four separate compartments behind the four faces.
misconceptions.correction: The cube is one hollow container of water, which puts every face at the same temperature. That is the whole design of the apparatus: it removes temperature as a variable so that the nature of the surface is the only thing left to explain the difference.

misconceptions.question: Does the distance between the surface and the infrared detector need to be kept the same?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The detector reading falls as it is moved away, so the distance must be identical for every face or the comparison is worthless.
misconceptions.misconception: Distance does not matter as long as the detector is pointing at the face, so it is fine to move it closer to get a clearer reading.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students see the detector as reading a property of the surface rather than as measuring the radiation arriving at one particular place, so its position looks like a matter of convenience.
misconceptions.correction: The detector measures the infrared arriving where it stands, which depends on distance as well as on the surface. Fix the distance with a ruler and keep it for all four faces, so that the surface is the only variable being changed.

misconceptions.question: A wall does not transmit visible light. Does that mean it absorbs all of it?
misconceptions.correct: No. Some of the light is reflected at the surface and some is absorbed. Not transmitted does not mean entirely absorbed.
misconceptions.misconception: There are only two things a wave can do at a substance — go through it or be absorbed by it — so anything not transmitted must have been absorbed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Absorption and transmission are usually introduced as a pair, while reflection is taught in a separate lesson about mirrors, so students do not hold all three possibilities in mind at once.
misconceptions.correction: A wave meeting a substance can be transmitted, absorbed or reflected, and in general all three happen in some proportion. You can see a wall at all precisely because it reflects a good deal of the light falling on it.

misconceptions.question: Which way does a ray bend as it passes from air into a glass block?
misconceptions.correct: Towards the normal, because light travels more slowly in glass than in air.
misconceptions.misconception: The ray bends away from the normal on entering the glass, and back towards the normal when it leaves.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two boundaries of a rectangular block look alike on a diagram, so the pair of bends is memorised as a shape without the rule that fixes which way round they go. Students then draw the pair in reverse.
misconceptions.correction: Tie the direction of bending to the change of speed: slowing down bends the ray towards the normal, speeding up bends it away. Air into glass is slowing down, so the ray bends towards the normal.

misconceptions.question: Do all electromagnetic waves travel at the same velocity in every substance?
misconceptions.correct: No. They all travel at the same velocity through a vacuum, but the velocity in a substance depends on the substance, and on the wavelength as well.
misconceptions.misconception: Electromagnetic waves always travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s, so their velocity can never differ from one substance to another.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The single value quoted for the speed of electromagnetic waves is learned without the phrase 'in a vacuum' attached to it, and it is repeated so often that it hardens into a universal constant of the wave itself.
misconceptions.correction: The common value applies in a vacuum, and very nearly in air. In glass or water the velocity is lower, and it is exactly that difference in velocity between two substances that causes refraction at the boundary.

misconceptions.question: If the wave slows down in the second medium, why does that turn it?
misconceptions.correct: Because the front does not slow all at once: one end crosses the boundary first and is held back while the other end is still moving at the old speed, so the front pivots.
misconceptions.misconception: The whole wave front crosses the boundary and slows down together, and slowing down by itself is what makes the wave change direction.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students correctly learn that refraction is caused by a change of speed and stop there, without asking why a change of speed should produce a change of direction rather than simply a slower wave.
misconceptions.correction: A change of speed alone does not turn a wave — a wave meeting the boundary head-on slows without deviating. Turning needs the two ends of the front to be moving at different speeds for a moment, which only happens when the front meets the boundary at an angle.

misconceptions.question: Is the angle of refraction the angle between the incident ray and the refracted ray?
misconceptions.correct: No. The angle of refraction is measured between the refracted ray and the normal, on the far side of the boundary.
misconceptions.misconception: The angle of refraction means the amount by which the ray has been bent, so it is the angle between the ray's old direction and its new one.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The everyday sense of 'refraction' is the bending itself, so 'angle of refraction' is read as 'angle of bend'. On a diagram both rays are already drawn in, which makes that the easy angle to measure.
misconceptions.correction: Both named angles are measured from the normal: the angle of incidence between the incident ray and the normal, the angle of refraction between the refracted ray and the normal. The angle of bend is the difference between them and has no name in the specification.

misconceptions.question: Which surface takes in infrared radiation fastest — matt black or polished silver?
misconceptions.correct: Matt black. A polished silver surface reflects most of the infrared falling on it and is the poorest absorber of the four usual surfaces.
misconceptions.misconception: Shiny metal takes radiation in best, because metals feel cold to touch and warm up quickly, so they must be good at drawing energy in.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students merge radiation with conduction. A metal does feel cold and does conduct well, and that experience is transferred to a question about radiation, where the polished surface in fact reflects.
misconceptions.correction: Conduction and radiation are different transfers. What matters for infrared arriving at a surface is whether the surface absorbs or reflects it: matt black absorbs almost all of it, polished silver reflects almost all of it.

misconceptions.question: A ray enters a glass block at an angle to the normal. Does it just slow down and carry straight on?
misconceptions.correct: No. Because it meets the boundary at an angle it also changes direction, bending towards the normal as it slows.
misconceptions.misconception: Entering glass only changes the wave's speed, so a slanted ray simply slows down and continues in a straight line.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn that refraction is caused by a change of speed and conclude that speed is the only thing that changes, so the change of direction that gives refraction its name is dropped.
misconceptions.correction: A change of speed at an angled boundary produces a change of direction: one end of the wave front is slowed before the other, so a slanted ray bends towards the normal rather than continuing straight.

misconceptions.question: When a ray of light meets the surface of a glass block at an angle, does it bounce off instead of going in?
misconceptions.correct: No. Glass transmits visible light, so most of the ray crosses into the block and is refracted; it does not simply reflect off the surface.
misconceptions.misconception: A ray meeting a glass surface reflects off it, like light from a mirror, rather than passing into the glass and refracting.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Reflection at a shiny surface is met before refraction, and a glass block looks reflective, so students expect the ray to bounce rather than enter and bend.
misconceptions.correction: A transparent block transmits most of the light reaching it, and that light crosses the boundary and refracts. Some reflection does occur, but only for a small part of the ray, which is not what a refraction ray diagram shows.

mcqs.stem: A sheet of window glass lets almost all of the visible light reaching it pass through, but it absorbs most of the ultraviolet. What does this show?

options.text: Whether a substance absorbs or transmits a wave can depend on the wavelength of that wave.
options.rationale: Different substances may absorb, transmit, refract or reflect electromagnetic waves in ways that vary with wavelength, and one substance treating two wavelengths differently is exactly that.

options.text: A material that looks clear to the eye must be transmitting every wave reaching it.
options.rationale: Treats transparency as a property of the material as a whole, so 'glass is see-through' is read as a claim about the entire spectrum.

options.text: Ultraviolet is absorbed by every substance it meets, whatever that substance is.
options.rationale: Attaches the behaviour to the wave alone and ignores the substance; quartz and air both transmit ultraviolet.

options.text: Any wave the glass does not transmit must be completely absorbed by it.
options.rationale: Holding a transmit-or-absorb model, the student concludes untransmitted ultraviolet must be entirely absorbed.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about how substances behave towards electromagnetic waves is correct?

options.text: A substance that fails to transmit a wave must have absorbed the whole of it.
options.rationale: Leaves reflection out of the list of possibilities, so 'not transmitted' collapses into 'absorbed'.

options.text: One substance can reflect one wavelength but absorb a different one.
options.rationale: This is what the specification means by behaviour varying with wavelength: a single substance treats different wavelengths differently.

options.text: A wave behaves in just the same way in every substance it meets.
options.rationale: Makes behaviour a property of the wave alone, which is contradicted by radio passing through brick but not through metal.

options.text: A clear substance will transmit every wavelength reaching it.
options.rationale: Generalises visible transparency to the whole spectrum; clear glass still absorbs much of the ultraviolet.

mcqs.stem: Radio waves from a distant transmitter pass easily through the brick walls of a house, but visible light from outside does not. Which explanation is best?

options.text: Radio waves carry far more energy than light, so they force a way through brick.
options.rationale: Explains the difference by the wave alone, and inverts the energy order as well: radio carries the least energy per photon of all.

options.text: Brick is not transparent, so no electromagnetic wave at all can cross it.
options.rationale: Applies the everyday meaning of transparency to the whole spectrum, which the stem itself contradicts.

options.text: The brick transmits radio waves but reflects and absorbs the light.
options.rationale: The same substance behaves differently towards different wavelengths, which is precisely the variation with wavelength the specification describes.

options.text: The light is not transmitted, so the wall absorbs every bit of it.
options.rationale: Forgets reflection; you can see the wall only because a good deal of the light bounces off it.

mcqs.stem: A water wave crosses from deep water into shallow water at an angle to the boundary and changes direction. What causes the change of direction?

options.text: The wave bounces off the edge of the shallow part and is pushed aside.
options.rationale: Invents a mechanical push at the boundary, the usual substitute for a cause when the change of speed is not noticed.

options.text: The shallow water blocks part of the wave, so the rest swings round.
options.rationale: Nothing is blocked; the whole wave crosses the boundary, and it is the difference in velocity that pivots it.

options.text: The two depths pull on the wave with different sideways forces.
options.rationale: Treats the boundary as exerting a force on the wave rather than as a place where the velocity of the wave changes.

options.text: The wave has a different velocity in the shallower water.
options.rationale: Some effects, for example refraction, are due to the difference in velocity of the waves in different substances.

mcqs.stem: Light travelling through air enters a glass block, where it travels more slowly. Its frequency does not change. What happens to its wavelength?

options.text: It stays the same, because the wavelength is fixed by the lamp producing it.
options.rationale: Holds the wrong quantity constant: the source fixes the frequency, and the medium then fixes the wavelength.

options.text: It gets shorter, because the velocity falls while the frequency stays the same.
options.rationale: With the velocity smaller and the frequency unchanged, the wavelength must fall, so the wave fronts sit closer together in the glass.

options.text: It gets longer, because a slower wave needs more time for each cycle.
options.rationale: The time for each cycle is set by the frequency, which has not changed; only the distance covered in that time has.

options.text: It stays the same, because light has one fixed speed in everything.
options.rationale: The fixed speed applies in a vacuum; the stem has already stated that the light is slower inside the glass.

mcqs.stem: A student is drawing a ray diagram for light passing from air into a glass block. Where should the angle of incidence be measured?

options.text: Between the incoming ray and the flat surface of the glass block itself.
options.rationale: Measures from the line already drawn rather than from the normal, giving an angle that is 90° minus the correct one.

options.text: Between the incoming ray and the refracted ray inside the block.
options.rationale: That angle is the amount of bend, which the specification does not name; both named angles run to the normal.

options.text: Between the incoming ray and the normal drawn at the point it enters.
options.rationale: The normal is the dashed line at right angles to the boundary at the point of entry, and both angles are measured from it.

options.text: Between the refracted ray and the flat surface of the block.
options.rationale: Uses the wrong ray and the wrong reference line at once; the angle of incidence belongs to the incident ray.

mcqs.stem: A ray of light travels from air into a glass block along the normal, so the angle of incidence is 0°. What should the ray diagram show?

options.text: The ray bends towards the normal as it enters, then bends back as it leaves.
options.rationale: The standard slanted-ray picture applied where it does not belong; at 0° the whole wave front arrives together.

options.text: The ray bends away from the normal as soon as it crosses into the glass.
options.rationale: Reverses the rule as well as ignoring the 0° case: slowing down bends a ray towards the normal, not away from it.

options.text: The ray bends sideways as soon as it enters the glass block.
options.rationale: Believing glass always bends light, the student draws a sideways bend even at 0 degree incidence.

options.text: The ray carries straight on through the block without changing course.
options.rationale: Along the normal every part of the wave front crosses the boundary at the same instant, so the wave slows but is not deviated.

mcqs.stem: In a wave front diagram, what does each drawn line represent?

options.text: A line joining points of the wave that are all in phase.
options.rationale: A wave front joins points in phase, such as all the crests, and it lies at right angles to the direction of travel.

options.text: A line drawn parallel to the direction the wave is travelling.
options.rationale: That is how a ray is drawn; wave fronts are perpendicular to rays, not parallel to them.

options.text: A line whose spacing is the same in every medium it enters.
options.rationale: The spacing is the wavelength, which changes with the speed when the wave crosses into a new medium.

options.text: A line that is spaced more widely wherever the wave moves slower.
options.rationale: Thinking that slowing a wave spreads its fronts apart, the student defines a front by speed-dependent spacing.

mcqs.stem: A wave front diagram shows plane wave fronts meeting a boundary at an angle. The wave travels more slowly in the second medium. Why do the fronts change direction?

options.text: The whole of each front slows down at the very same instant it crosses.
options.rationale: If a front slowed all at once it would simply travel more slowly in a straight line; nothing would turn it.

options.text: The fronts turn because the ray drawn through them is refracted there.
options.rationale: Circular: the bent ray records the refraction rather than causing it, and the ray only follows where the fronts go.

options.text: One end of each front enters the slower medium first and is held back, so it pivots.
options.rationale: While one end is slowed and the other is still at the original speed the front swings round, which is the wave front explanation of refraction.

options.text: The fronts spread further apart in the slower medium, and that turns them.
options.rationale: The fronts move closer together, not further apart, and their spacing is not what changes the direction.

mcqs.stem: In Required practical activity 10 a Leslie cube is filled with hot water. An infrared detector is placed the same distance from each vertical face in turn. Which face gives the highest reading?

options.text: All four read the same, because the water behind each face is at one temperature.
options.rationale: The equal temperature is what makes the comparison fair; the surfaces still differ, so the readings differ.

options.text: The shiny silver face, because polished metal gives out infrared best.
options.rationale: Polished silver is the poorest emitter of the four, and the poorest absorber as well.

options.text: The matt white face, because pale surfaces give out the most radiation.
options.rationale: Pale matt surfaces sit between black and silver; matt black, not white, is the best emitter.

options.text: The matt black face, because matt black is the best emitter of infrared.
options.rationale: A good absorber is also a good emitter, so the matt black face radiates most strongly at that temperature.

mcqs.stem: A student compares the infrared radiation emitted by the four faces of a Leslie cube. Which change would most improve the investigation?

options.text: Keep the detector the same distance from every face when reading it.
options.rationale: Distance is a control variable: the reading falls as the detector is moved away, so it must be fixed if only the surface is to change.

options.text: Move the detector closer to the darker faces so their readings are clearer.
options.rationale: Changes two things at once, so a larger reading could be caused by the shorter distance rather than by the surface.

options.text: Take the reading from each of the faces at a different water temperature.
options.rationale: Temperature strongly affects emission, so varying it alongside the surface makes the comparison meaningless.

options.text: Use a separate metal cube for each of the four surfaces tested.
options.rationale: Four cubes introduce differences in water temperature and in cooling; the single cube exists precisely to remove them.

mcqs.stem: Four identical cans are painted matt black, matt white, shiny silver and dull grey. Each is filled with cold water and placed the same distance from a radiant heater. Which can's water warms fastest?

options.text: The shiny silver can, because a polished metal surface takes radiation in best.
options.rationale: Confuses conduction with radiation; a polished surface reflects most of the infrared reaching it.

options.text: The matt black can, because it is the best absorber of infrared.
options.rationale: Matt black is the best absorber, so it takes in radiation from the heater at the greatest rate and warms fastest.

options.text: All four cans equally, because the heater is the same distance away.
options.rationale: Equal distance makes the test fair; the surfaces still differ, and it is the surface that sets the rate of absorption.

options.text: The dull grey can, because a metal surface draws radiation in fastest.
options.rationale: Reading the dull grey can as metal, the student thinks metals draw radiation in fastest.

mcqs.stem: A ray of light travels through air and strikes the flat surface of a glass block at an angle to the normal. Light travels more slowly in glass than in air. Which statement correctly describes the refracted ray inside the glass?

options.text: It bends towards the normal, because it slows down in the glass.
options.rationale: Air into glass is a change to a slower medium, and a ray slowing at an angled boundary bends towards the normal.

options.text: It bends away from the normal as it enters the glass.
options.rationale: Reverses the rule: bending away from the normal is what happens on entering a faster medium, not a slower one.

options.text: It carries straight on undeviated, changing only its speed.
options.rationale: The speed does fall, but at an angled boundary that change of speed also turns the ray; only a ray along the normal carries straight on.

options.text: It reflects off the surface without entering the glass at all.
options.rationale: Glass transmits visible light, so most of the ray enters and refracts; only a small part is reflected, which a refraction diagram does not show.
